blocks.text: If you’re really serious about getting fit, with all the benefits that it brings, there is one thing you will have to give up: Smoking.
There’s no painless or effortless way to stop smoking, but linking it to your efforts to keep fit gives you a positive excuse to kick the habit once and for all.

Few smokers who quit on a sudden impulse ever succeed. A similar impulse occurs and they start smoking again. Usually, to be successful, a really conscious effort is needed, in the time for that conscious effort. Now with good health as your goal.

items: * Cigarettes are dangerous. Medical research has proved it.
* Smoking reduces your ability to do vigorous exercise.
* Cigarettes cause bronchitis and increase the risk of coronary heart disease and emphysema.
* Cigarettes may complicate pregnancy.

blocks.text: Draw up a ‘stop smoking action plan’ to run alongside your efforts to get fit.
Underline the word in parenthesis which completes the meaning of the sentence.

items: If you want to get and keep fit, you should not (run – eat – sweat – smoke).
When you give up doing something, you (stop – start – continue – sweat – smoke) doing it.
Women are advised not to smoke because medical research has found that cigarettes may cause (pain – pleasure – harm – bronchitis) to the fetus.
For most smokers, to stop smoking is not (easy – hard – dangerous – healthy).

items.q: Would you like your children to smoke?
Why is it necessary to stop smoking if you want to keep fit?
Are you in favor of or against cigarette advertising on television? Why?
Will you allow other people to smoke when they are near you? Give reasons to support your answer.

blocks.title: Do You Mind if I Smoke?

items: *Peggy:* It’s twelve thirty. It’s time to go to lunch.
*Jane:* Yes. Let’s stop working and go to the cafeteria downstairs.
*Peggy:* What would you like to eat?
*Jane:* I only want a plain hamburger. I really shouldn’t eat too much.
*Peggy:* Are you on a diet?
*Jane:* No, I just want to be a little careful. By the way, I have to ask you something.
*Peggy:* What is it?
*Jane:* Are you going to smoke?
*Peggy:* Why do you ask?
*Jane:* Well, I couldn’t sit with a person who smokes. I’m sorry, but I just couldn’t.
*Peggy:* What’s the matter with you? Oh, I see. You must’ve given up smoking! Is that it?
*Jane:* Yes, I haven’t smoked for a week.
*Peggy:* Well, good for you! Smoking is really harmful for your health. I think I’ll try to give it up too.
*Jane:* There’s only one way to give it up and that’s just stop.
*Peggy:* Yes, you’re right. But can I have at least one last cigarette?
*Jane:* Oh, no. If you don’t do it now, you never will.
*Peggy:* All right. Let’s go. I hope there aren’t going to be a lot of people smoking in the cafeteria.
*Jane:* We shouldn’t sit near the smokers. That’s all.

blocks.text: Write a dialogue between a habitual drinker and his wife, each one defending his point of view. (See function below)

items: *a)* I insist…
*b)* There’s no doubt that…
*c)* Sorry, but…
*d)* You may have a point, but…
*e)* Don’t be silly.. I can’t accept…
*f)* That’s nonsense…
*g)* I can’t possibly agree with you
*h)* I really can’t agree with you, are you crazy?
*i)* You’ve got to be kidding.
*j)* You can’t be serious…
*k)* Come on, that’s ridiculous.
